doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: Leaving the church and Reverend Turner's taste in music
summary: Ware drifts out of the church as he plays with the older boys; Turner disapproves and steers him toward country music and white radio bands.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Were you still playing in the church at this time, or had you completely gotten out of it?
Well, I didn't believe in mixing the two,

but by that time when I started with those older boys in the neighborhood, they come around and asked Ms. Turner could I go out with them, and I just kind of dropped out of the church. In fact, the church just seemed like it kind of disintegrated; I don't know what happened. But I didn't go back to the church.
What did Reverend Turner think of your playing with these bands?

Oh, he would say, 'That was a mess.' See, Reverend Turner was a strange musical man, and he had his beliefs. Now on Saturday nights, his favorite music movie was the 8th Street Theatre -- to me, that was a forerunner of this Grand Old Opry. Every Saturday night when I wasn't out hustling with the various new groups, he'd say, 'Now that's the kind of music you should listen to.' And I got a whole lot of the old Hoosier Hotshots; that's another side of it -- the music was beautiful. We had bands coming from the Black Hawk Restaurant down there in Chicago, Art Jarrett Gerard and I think Lawrence Welk used to broadcast. And later on, in the thirties, the Hotel Sherman, they were bringing big bands in.
